entities.summary: Pope Paul I, who reigned as the bishop of Rome and sovereign of the nascent Papal States from May 29, 757, until his death on June 28, 767, was a pivotal figure in the consolidation of papal temporal power and the deepening schism between Rome and Byzantium. Succeeding his brother, Stephen II, Paul I inherited and vigorously pursued the Frankish alliance forged by his predecessor, which was instrumental in securing the territorial foundations of the Papacy against continued Lombard encroachment and Byzantine political influence in Italy. His pontificate marks a critical decade where the Roman See solidified its independent political identity, navigating the complex geopolitical landscape of an unraveling Byzantine exarchate, an ascendant Frankish kingdom, and a persistent Lombard threat. He was instrumental in establishing the Papacy as a distinct temporal power in central Italy, laying groundwork for future papal claims.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Paul I's pontificate solidified the Frankish-Papal alliance and secured the nascent Papal States, profoundly influencing the geopolitical landscape of medieval Europe and setting the stage for future papal temporal power. His actions further widened the schism between the Roman and Byzantine Churches.
